description: I Am The Cavalry talks from BSides Las Vegas 2022.

talks.title: Rivers on Fire; Shaping the next phase of the mission
talks.teaser: Surveys how cyberattacks on hospitals, water, food and fuel have caused real harm and what policy followed.
talks.summary:
The session opens by framing cyberattacks on hospitals, water utilities, food processing, fuel pipelines and local governments as a present-day problem rather than a theoretical one. The speakers describe a gap between well-resourced organizations and "target rich, cyber poor" operators who have no security staff. They tie a 2021 analysis of excess deaths to delayed time-sensitive care during ransomware disruption, and they use ICU capacity strain as a leading indicator of that harm.

The middle of the talk reviews nearly a decade of progress. Examples include an automotive safety framework that carmakers and regulators later drew on, FDA premarket and postmarket guidance that mirrors a published oath for connected medical devices, a 2020 US law setting minimum security standards for IoT purchases, and federal requirements for coordinated vulnerability disclosure. The speakers also point to a published list of bad practices, such as running unsupported end-of-life software in critical infrastructure and relying on hard-coded or guessable maintenance passwords, which they hope will shape insurance and legal standards.

The closing segment urges attendees to change how the public discusses attacks, focusing on patient access and public safety rather than record counts or fines. It also calls for tools, volunteer roles and back-office support to help under-resourced operators. The practical takeaway is that practitioners can help smaller organizations by supporting software bill of materials work and by joining local, state or sector efforts.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from the CISA COVID Task Force & Healthcare Attacks
talks.teaser: Presents how a federal COVID-19 task force prioritized healthcare and supply chain targets for cyber protection.
talks.summary:
The session recounts how a CISA task force formed during the COVID-19 pandemic started with a list of more than a thousand companies and no set method for deciding which to protect first. The speakers describe adapting a wartime idea of focusing on the critical weak points in a chain. Entities were scored on product type, how scarce the product was, supply levels, and dependencies, such as the specialized lipids needed by nucleic acid vaccines. The scored list was sorted into tiers so a small cybersecurity team could concentrate on the most critical organizations.

The talk then turns to healthcare. Ransomware attacks on hospitals disrupted electronic records, communications, and the processing of test results, and the team's research linked these effects to excess deaths, with the steepest increases among adults aged 25 to 44. Outreach to small manufacturers and hospitals often met suspicion, and many of these organizations had no security staff or incident response plans. The team responded with free services and plain guidance aimed at smaller healthcare providers and related sectors.

The closing lessons focus on organization. Outside perspectives and nimble, cross-agency teams helped, crisis conditions made it possible to pilot new approaches, and breaking down silos between agencies such as the FBI took sustained effort. The speakers also argue that practitioners should describe security risk in terms of business impact so that leaders act on it.

talks.title: STUFF is on Fire - a Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists walk through ransomware, misconfigurations and risk across water, food and municipal critical infrastructure.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with two cloud incidents that the speakers describe as largely avoidable. In one, an admin account without working multi-factor authentication had a weak password that leaked to GitHub, and attackers used it to spin up crypto-mining virtual machines that raised monthly spend sharply. In the other, a misconfigured network security group left a cloud environment open, and an outside party took hundreds of gigabytes of data and threatened public disclosure. Both were framed as human error that basic checks and staffing could have prevented. The discussion then turns to risk: panelists argue that organizations should start from their mission, identify the assets and processes that support it, and explain impact to business leaders in their own terms.

The middle section moves through critical infrastructure sectors. A water-sector speaker describes funding gaps, aging pipe, workforce loss and the cultural gap between utilities and private industry, and notes that a left-on legacy machine enabled tampering at one plant. The food and agriculture discussion focuses on concentration risk, citing a meat processor hit by ransomware that stopped production and a single infant formula plant whose shutdown caused shortages. It also covers connected tractors that collect large volumes of farm data in centralized portals. Municipal and school examples show segmentation helping one city, while a county and a school district lost services and struggled with unclear responsibilities. The speakers also challenge common assumptions, including the Purdue model, the idea of an air gap, and the labeling of every scan as an attack.

The closing takeaways stress rehearsing response through tabletop exercises, since the Colonial Pipeline shutdown was attributed to unpracticed fear. Attendees are urged to join local utility board meetings, ask about risks, and share information across sectors. The panel also points to the ICS FOR ICS response framework as a standardization effort for industrial incidents.

talks.title: Target Rich Cyber Poor
talks.teaser: Presents federal no-cost security services and guidance aimed at small, under-resourced critical infrastructure organizations.
talks.summary:
The session looks at a gap the speakers call target rich, cyber poor: hospitals, utilities and small businesses that support critical functions but have little or no dedicated security staff. The speakers said their no-cost vulnerability assessments kept finding the same weaknesses, and they mapped those findings to MITRE ATT&CK to show how attackers got in.

The middle of the talk walks through free federal resources that smaller organizations can use. The Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and its update alerts come first, followed by Cyber Hygiene services for scanning internet-facing assets, the standalone Cyber Security Evaluation Tool for self-assessment, and state-based cyber advisors who can visit in person. The team also reviewed a short list of bad practices: unsupported software, default passwords and single-factor remote or administrative access. Audience members pushed for sector-specific guidance, business cases that let non-technical staff request budget, and matching volunteers with under-resourced organizations.

The takeaway is that free services exist but are underused, so organizations need to be persuaded that security is a business risk rather than an IT chore. The speakers suggested framing security as continuity and insurance for leadership, and building sector-specific playbooks, with practitioners in the room helping draft them.

talks.title: The Hip Hacker's Guide to Policy
talks.teaser: Walks through how US policy is made and how hackers can influence it, plus recent legal changes for security research.
talks.summary:
A panel from the I Am The Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas 2022 set out to explain how policy gets made, starting with a simplified tour of the three branches of the US government. The speakers described how Congress writes laws, how regulatory agencies create rules through public comment, and why executive orders depend on existing statutory authority. They argued that influence is possible at several points in this cycle, including committee staff, rulemaking comments, and coordinated letters that gain weight when many organizations sign on.

The middle of the session covered legal protections for security research. The panel traced how the DMCA exemption for research was created and renewed through the Library of Congress process, and how the Department of Justice later issued guidance telling federal prosecutors to decline good-faith research cases under the computer fraud statute. They also discussed vulnerability disclosure policies as a practical way for organizations to authorize testing, and noted that state laws differ. The IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act and newer federal reporting and zero trust efforts were presented as signs of a growing government appetite for cybersecurity regulation.

The takeaway for practitioners is that framing matters. Legal arguments focus on conduct and research outcomes rather than on whether someone calls themselves a researcher. Specific, technical comments on draft language are more useful to policymakers than general opposition, and state-level developments are worth sharing through community channels. The panel acknowledged that defining good faith remains hard and encouraged the community to help articulate norms for responsible research.

talks.title: Day One Feedback Loop: What did we hear?
talks.teaser: Looks back at a day of Cavalry talks on critical infrastructure and asks how the group's mission should evolve.
talks.summary:
This session is a feedback round held at the end of the first day of I Am The Cavalry's track at BSidesLV 2022. Josh Corman opens by recapping the day's talks, which covered how critical infrastructure risk has grown over nine years, from healthcare and vaccine supply chains to water, food, energy, schools and municipal services. He also reviews recent policy changes, including the situation facing good-faith security research, and poses the open question of whether the group's original mission is complete or whether it should change.

The middle of the session is an audience speed round. Attendees raise themes such as the gap between well-funded organizations and under-resourced operators, the concentration of risk in a few large vendors and facilities, and the lack of diversity in who takes part in security work. Others argue that connected devices and software should be treated as public infrastructure, that vendors' incentives favor cheap products over secure ones, and that the field needs better metrics to show whether security is actually improving. Corman responds with examples, including unsupported Exchange servers in hospitals and the value of measurable confidence-building practices such as patchability, vulnerability disclosure programs and software bills of materials.

The closing portion turns to the tension between private commercial interests and public good, with proposals for an opt-in designation for public-interest security work and debate over whether consolidation or diversification better protects essential services. Corman concludes that progress is real but outpaced by adversary activity, and he asks attendees to bring ideas to the next day's brainstorm on possible open-source tools for under-resourced organizations.

talks.title: M33t the Press: CyberSafety Got Real: Now What?
talks.teaser: Two technology reporters discuss how security coverage of infrastructure risk has changed and why public-interest stories are hard to tell.
talks.summary:
This fireside chat, part of the I Am The Cavalry track at BSides Las Vegas 2022, features Wired's Lily Hayne Newman and SC Media's Joe Uchill reflecting on how security coverage has changed since the group began warning about connected infrastructure nine years earlier. The moderator frames the discussion around the gap between early warnings, made before harm had been proven, and today's reports of attacks on water, fuel, schools and patient care.

The panelists compare the news environment of roughly 2013 with the present. Early coverage tended to focus on breaches and record-sized attacks, while today's reporting is driven by individual incidents and the need for daily output. They describe a thinning of specialist beats, many experienced reporters moving into corporate or PR roles, and a heavy reliance on enterprise-focused publications whose readers want guidance for their own organisations rather than public-interest analysis. Multi-disciplinary stories about supply chains or public-private responsibility for utilities are hard to staff. Ransomware is discussed as a business model that has grown faster than efforts to stop it.

Later the conversation turns to international coverage and language barriers, and to why slow-moving risks such as healthcare disruption get less attention than a single named victim. The panelists suggest wider source networks, earlier relationships between researchers and reporters, and fiction or documentaries as ways to reach the public. The takeaway is that public-interest reporting needs time, expertise and sustained attention.

talks.title: #SBOM is here: making progress (not excuses)
talks.teaser: A panel of healthcare and standards practitioners discusses where software bill of materials adoption stands and what comes next.
talks.summary:
The panel opens with why software bill of materials (SBOM) matter, especially in safety-critical sectors such as medical devices and industrial control systems. Patching is hard there, and buyers often cannot see what components a product contains. The speakers compare an SBOM to an ingredient list: it does not fix anything by itself, but it lets organizations judge risk, including the transitive dependencies that no one tracks by hand.

The discussion then traces several years of multi-stakeholder working groups that moved from defining SBOMs to making them usable. Topics include the SPDX and CycloneDX data formats, VEX statements about whether a vulnerability actually affects a product, cloud and SaaS scope, and ways to share SBOMs with customers without exposing them publicly. A hospital team presents DaggerBoard, an open-source analysis tool that ingests SPDX or CycloneDX files, maps packages to known vulnerabilities, assigns each SBOM a grade, and supports LDAP sign-in and adjustable grading. A recorded demo walks through the dashboard, vendor grouping and admin settings. The roadmap adds VEX support, an API for asset management and CI/CD systems, and global CVE search across stored SBOMs.

The closing advice is practical. Ask vendors for machine-readable SBOMs during procurement, use standard questionnaires where possible, and treat SBOMs as a basis for ongoing risk decisions. The panelists also stress that smaller, resource-poor organizations need simple tools and guidance, and they invite developers to contribute to open projects.

talks.title: ICS Security Assessments 101 or How da Fox I Test Dis?
talks.teaser: Walks through a consultant's approach to assessing industrial control systems, from process familiarization to safe active testing.
talks.summary:
The talk is an introduction to security assessments of industrial control systems, aimed at consultants who may be asked to test operational technology environments. The speaker explains why ICS devices such as PLCs, RTUs and SCADA software tend to be weaker than IT systems, pointing to legacy design, missing authentication and poor separation between IT and OT networks. Rather than offering a full methodology, the talk maps practical examples onto the steps of a published approach.

The middle sections cover the assessment stages: setting security priorities, learning how the process runs through interviews and walkthroughs, and checking gaps against the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and a cybersecurity evaluation tool. Passive work includes analysing Modbus traffic and reviewing devices through their web interfaces, where default credentials were found. Demos show recovered credentials from an older Siemens PLC and manipulated sensor data sent over the S7 protocol to a test device without disturbing the master controller.

The closing section describes a mining red team engagement where ventilation systems were excluded because online testing could endanger workers, while offline proximity and tracking devices were analysed instead. The takeaways are to understand the operating context, test passively and escalate carefully, and report findings that add real value, such as poor IT and OT communication, unclear ownership of fixes and missing OT coverage in security programs, rather than generic issues the industry already knows.

talks.title: We're not from the government, but we're here to help them help you
talks.teaser: Explains how volunteer cyber defense groups help public bodies and nonprofits recover from attacks and build resilience.
talks.summary:
The session, given by two speakers from volunteer cyber defense programs, explains how civilian experts can support public bodies and nonprofits that lack dedicated security staff. The first speaker described a Michigan volunteer corps formed with state backing in the early 2010s. Many of the state's public entities have little or no IT support, and a statewide exercise exposed gaps in coordinated response. The group explained its selection path, which includes skills tests, background checks, and agreements with both the volunteer and the volunteer's employer. Members train together and respond only when a victim formally requests help, with state police and a cyber command unit handling the legal side.

The second speaker, from a Geneva-based nonprofit, outlined the growing targeting of humanitarian organizations, where attacks have diverted funds and exposed personal data of vulnerable people. Its Cyber Peace Builders program pairs security professionals with short, mostly remote missions for these groups, ranging from code reviews to one-hour assessments. Volunteers do not all need technical roles, and the work is mostly before or after an incident rather than during one.

The main takeaway is that people respond to reassurance as much as to facts, so outreach should be human and local. Organizations can encourage staff to volunteer through formal employer agreements, and the panel closed by discussing how independent volunteer groups could link up across regions.
